title: Telling your project in five minutes
promise: You'll prepare the explanation of your project so it lands without any technical knowledge: what problem it solves, how much it saves and what people see working. By the end you'll have rehearsed it and timed it with someone in front of you.
why: Álvaro pitched his project to a clinic looking to automate bookings. He started by explaining that he used n8n with a webhook, an OpenAI node and a database. Two minutes in, the person making the decision was looking at their phone. They weren't interested in the plumbing: they wanted to know how many calls their receptionist would be spared. Álvaro had the figure, he had measured it, and he said it at minute seven, when nobody was listening any more.

theory.title: Nobody buys the technology, they buy the problem solved
theory.text: When you show something you've built, the temptation is to start with what it cost you: the tool, the steps, what you learned along the way. It's human and it's the worst possible order. Whoever is listening is solving a question of their own, not yours, and that question is «is this any use to me?». Until you answer it, everything else is surplus. The rule is simple: start with the problem and who it hurts, carry on with what changes, and leave the technology for when someone asks. If nobody asks, it didn't need telling.
theory.analogy: Nobody buys a drill for the motor. They buy it for the hole, and not even that: for the shelf on the wall.
theory.example: Álvaro should have started with «your receptionist takes about forty calls a day; this takes half of them away». The word n8n never needed saying.

theory.title: The five-minute order
theory.text: There's an order that works and it's five one-minute stretches. First: what the problem is and who it hurts, with a concrete scene, not a category. Second: what happens now without this, with a number. Third: showing it working, for real, not on slides. Fourth: what changes, with the same number from before, changed. And fifth: what's needed to have it and what it doesn't do. That fifth stretch, the limits, is what makes them believe the four before it. If you're short of time, cut the third, not the first.
theory.example: «Forty calls a day, most of them asking opening hours. [shows the WhatsApp answering] Now twenty of those go. You need a WhatsApp Business number and about $25 a month. It doesn't change appointments and it doesn't give medical advice: it hands those over.»
theory.analogy: Telling someone about a film: you don't start with the cast or the budget. You start with who it happens to and what happens, which is why it lands in one sentence.

theory.title: The number has to be yours and measured
theory.text: What turns a demo into a proposal is a number, and it has to be from your case, not from an article. «Companies save 30% with AI» means nothing and everyone has heard it. «I counted the calls over three days: 118, and 71 of them were about opening hours» does mean something, because it can be checked and because it's from here. If you don't have the number, measure it before you present: two days of counting things by hand is worth more than any argument. And give the honest number, including what it doesn't save: that's precisely what makes the rest credible.
theory.example: Álvaro counted for three days. 71 of 118 calls were about opening hours and prices. His assistant resolved 58 of those 71. The rest were handed over. That's the figure, with both its numbers.
theory.analogy: "House prices have gone up a lot" is nothing. "Mine went from 700 to 950 in two years" anyone understands, and nobody argues with it, because it's yours and it's measured.

theory.title: Showing it working, with one thing that goes wrong
theory.text: A live demonstration is worth more than any explanation, and there are two ways to do it well. The first: showing the real path end to end, with data that resembles the real thing. The second, which almost nobody does and which impresses far more: deliberately showing a case your setup doesn't resolve, and how it hands it to a person. That demonstrates two things at once, that you know your limits and that you've thought about failure. And it takes off the table the awkward question they were going to ask anyway.
theory.example: Álvaro shows an opening-hours question (it answers), and then one saying «it hurts when I walk, should I come in?» (it hands it to him with a message). The second is the one that convinces.
theory.analogy: The market-stall seller demonstrating an air fryer switches it on right there and cooks a chip. They don't show a leaflet: they show the chip. And when asked what it can't do, they say so.

theory.title: Preparing the three questions that always come
theory.text: It's nearly always the same three and it's worth carrying them answered in one sentence each. What happens if it fails: you answer with what you built in block 08, the warnings and the undo. What happens with people's data: you answer with block 09, what goes in, what doesn't and what you checked about the provider. And how much it costs to maintain: you answer with the normal-month and bad-month sums. If you've done the earlier blocks, you already have all three answers written; you only have to cut them down to one sentence each.
theory.example: «If it fails, a warning reaches me the same day and I go back to the previous version in five minutes; I've timed it.» One sentence, and the subject is closed.
theory.analogy: The driving theory test: the questions are public and nearly always the same. Turning up unprepared isn't bad luck, it's not having looked at the syllabus.

theory.title: No slides if you can avoid it
theory.text: For five minutes, slides usually get in the way: they force you to look at the screen instead of at the person, and the time goes on advancing them. What works is one sheet with four things noted down in case you lose your thread, and the setup open and ready to show. If you have to take something written, make it the one-page document from the previous lesson: you leave it with them at the end and everything is there. What is worth preparing is the literal opening, the first sentence, because that's where people stall most.
theory.example: Álvaro's sheet: the call figure, the two demonstrations he's going to show, the three one-sentence answers, and what it costs a month. Four lines.
theory.analogy: Explaining something with a sheet of paper in your hand versus doing it while looking at the person. With the paper in front of you, you stop looking at whoever has to understand you.

tasks.title: Get your number
tasks.where: At work, over two or three days
tasks.action: If you don't have a measured figure for the problem you solve, measure it before anything else. Count by hand for two or three days: calls, emails, minutes, times you do something repetitive. Note the total and the share your setup takes. You need both numbers, not just the good one.
tasks.expect: Two figures from your case: how much there is and how much your setup resolves. For example «118 calls in 3 days, 71 were about opening hours, my assistant resolves 58».
tasks.stuck: If you can't measure the before because the setup is already running, look at the history: how many times it has run in the last month. That's what someone was doing by hand before.
tasks.prompt:
Help me get the number for my project, which is what turns a demo into a proposal.

WHAT PROBLEM MY PROJECT SOLVES: [DESCRIBE IT]
WHO SUFFERS IT TODAY AND HOW THEY DO IT NOW: [DESCRIBE IT]

Tell me what I have to count over two or three days to have a real figure, and make it concrete: what exactly I measure, how often I record it, and in what unit. Something I can count with a tally on paper, not an estimate.

Give me two options: the figure that's easy to measure even if rough, and the one that genuinely convinces even if it's more work. And tell me what does NOT count as a number: anything from an article, anything as a percentage without saying of what, and anything I couldn't explain how I measured if asked.

tasks.title: Write the five stretches
tasks.action: One sentence per stretch, in this order: the problem with a concrete scene, the number now, what you're going to show working, the number after, and what's needed and what it doesn't do. Five sentences. Also write out, word for word, the first sentence you'll open with.
tasks.expect: Five sentences and a literal opening. Read the whole thing aloud: it should take you under a minute. The five minutes come from what you explain around it.
tasks.stuck: If the first stretch comes out as a category («appointment management is inefficient»), bring it down to a scene: «your receptionist hangs up and it rings again, forty times a day».
tasks.prompt:
Help me write the five one-minute segments for telling people about my project.

THE PROBLEM AND WHO IT HURTS: [DESCRIBE IT]
MY CURRENT NUMBER: [THE MEASURED FIGURE]
WHAT I'LL SHOW WORKING: [DESCRIBE IT]
THE NUMBER AFTERWARDS: [THE FIGURE WITH THE BUILD]
WHAT I'M ASKING FOR AT THE END: [a meeting, a pilot, a decision]

Write me one sentence per segment, in that order, to be said out loud rather than read.

The first has to be a concrete scene with a person doing something on a particular day, not a category. The last has to be a clear ask with a date, not "if you're interested, let's talk". If any of my sentences sounds like a brochure, rewrite it and tell me why it sounded like one.

tasks.title: Prepare the two demonstrations
tasks.action: Prepare two cases ready to show live: one that works end to end with realistic data, and one your setup doesn't resolve and that hands over to a person. Have them written down and tested: no improvising in front of someone. And prepare the fallback, a thirty-second screen recording, in case the wifi fails or the service is down that very day.
tasks.expect: Two tested cases and a backup recording. The recording isn't pessimism: things fall over on demo day with suspicious frequency.
tasks.stuck: If your setup takes a while to respond live, prepare the case with the data already loaded up to the last step, and in the demonstration you only run that last one. It's honest as long as you say the earlier part was already prepared.
tasks.prompt:
Help me prepare the two live demos: the one that works and the one that doesn't.

WHAT MY BUILD DOES: [DESCRIBE IT]
WHAT DATA I'LL SHOW IT WITH: [real / invented]
WHAT I KNOW IT DOESN'T SOLVE: [DESCRIBE IT]

One: prepare the case that works start to finish. Tell me what concrete data to feed it so it looks realistic, how long it should take in front of someone, and what I say while it runs so the silence isn't awkward.
Two: prepare the case my build does NOT solve, and tell me how to present it so it doesn't look like a failure: what sentence I say before showing it and what I say afterwards.

And the important bit: tell me what can go wrong live (no internet, the service running slow, the test data having been deleted) and what I should have ready for each. I'd rather carry a backup screenshot than stand there watching a spinner.

tasks.title: Write the three one-sentence answers
tasks.action: What happens if it fails, what happens with the data, and how much it costs to maintain. One sentence each, taken from the files you already have from blocks 08 and 09. Make each one carry a fact: a time, a limit, a figure.
tasks.expect: Three sentences with a fact each. These are what separate a classroom project from one someone would consider paying for.
tasks.stuck: If you don't have one of the answers, don't invent it: say so. «I haven't measured that yet, I'll have it next week» is a perfectly good answer and far better than an improvised figure that doesn't add up later.
tasks.prompt:
Help me have one-sentence answers ready for the three questions that always come up.

WHAT I'VE WRITTEN ABOUT ALERTS AND ROLLBACK: [PASTE IT]
WHAT I'VE WRITTEN ABOUT DATA: [PASTE IT]
WHAT IT COSTS ME A MONTH: [AMOUNT]

Write me three answers, one sentence each, drawn from what I already have rather than invented:
1. What happens if it fails.
2. What happens with the data.
3. What it costs to keep running.

Each has to carry a concrete figure from my files, because an answer with a number gets believed and a general one doesn't. If what I've given you doesn't support a solid answer for any of the three, say so instead of padding it: I'd rather know my weak point before someone finds it in front of me.

tasks.title: Rehearse it with someone and time it
tasks.where: With a person outside your field
tasks.action: Tell the whole thing to someone with no idea about technology, with a timer running. At the end ask them three questions: what problem it solves, who for, and what it doesn't do. If they can't answer all three, the explanation isn't ready, however well it went for you.
tasks.expect: A time (the first go will run to eight or nine minutes) and three answers. Cut from the technical part until you're under five.
tasks.stuck: If your listener can't say who it's for, you skipped the first stretch or told it in the abstract. Go back to the concrete scene: one person, doing something, a number of times a day.
tasks.prompt:
Help me set up the timed rehearsal with someone who isn't technical.

MY FIVE SEGMENTS: [PASTE THEM]
WHO I'M REHEARSING WITH: [WHO]

One: tell me what to ask of them before starting, and what NOT to explain.
Two: give me the three exact questions to ask afterwards, to find out whether they understood the problem, whether they believed the number, and whether they could explain it to someone else.
Three: tell me what to note while I'm talking: where I ramble, where their attention drifts, and which segment eats my time.

And tell me what to do with the result: if I run over five minutes, which of the five segments gets cut first and which one never gets touched. If they didn't understand the problem, tell me the fault is in segment one and not the other four, because the temptation will be to add more explanation at the end.

tasks.title: Have the AI play the difficult audience
tasks.action: Give it your five sentences and ask it to put the awkward questions to you before a real person does.
tasks.prompt:
I'm presenting a project in five minutes to [WHO: a client, a manager, an examining panel]. They aren't technical people.

MY EXPLANATION:
[YOUR FIVE SENTENCES]
MY ANSWERS TO THE THREE USUAL QUESTIONS:
[THE THREE SENTENCES]

Play a sceptical audience, not a cheerleader:
1. The five awkward questions they'd ask me, ordered by likelihood. Write them the way that person would say them, in their words.
2. At exactly which point in my explanation would they switch off, and why.
3. Which part of what I say sounds like an unsupported promise.

Don't give me presentation tips and don't tell me to smile. Just the questions and the weak points.
tasks.expect: Five questions you will genuinely be asked. The commonest: «and what if it gets it wrong?», «doesn't the system we already have do this?» and «what happens when you're not around?».
tasks.stuck: If it gives you generic questions, say: «Take the part of [the specific person] and use their words.» When you give it the character, the questions get far more real.

matters: That you start with the problem and who it hurts, never with the tool.
That you need a measured number from your own case, not a statistic from an article.
That showing a case your setup doesn't resolve convinces more than showing five that it does.
That the three usual questions get carried answered in one sentence with a fact in it.
ignore: Slides for five minutes. They get in the way more than they help.
Explaining the architecture if nobody asks.
Industry statistics. Your three-day figure is worth more.
canDo: Tell your project in five minutes to someone who isn't technical.
Back what you say with a figure you measured yourself.
Show it working, including a case it doesn't resolve.
Answer in one sentence the three questions that always come up.
cantDo: Convince without a number of your own.
Improvise the demonstration: it has to be prepared, with a fallback.
Avoid the awkward questions: only arrive with them answered.
Know whether your explanation works without rehearsing it on an outsider.
words: Telling the problem through a person doing something, not through an abstract category.
The figure you measured from your own case. The only thing that backs a proposal.
Showing it genuinely working, with realistic data and a recorded fallback.
The example your setup doesn't resolve and passes to a person. What inspires the most confidence.
What happens if it fails, what happens with the data, how much it costs to maintain.
next: You know how to tell it. In lesson 47 you go to the next step: defending it when people ask in earnest, and answering what you don't know without going blank.
